paper.title: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1

paper_doc.title: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1
paper_doc.authors: Wei Liang, Marta Ortega, Hiroshi Nakamura · Department of Molecular Oncology, Fake Institute of Biomedical Engineering
paper_doc.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) spreads early within the liver, and the regulators of HCC cell motility are still poorly understood. MicroRNAs fine-tune many of these regulators. Here we examined miR-9071, a microRNA whose expression we found to be reduced in HCC tissue, and its predicted target SPAR1, a spindle-associated protein that is also found at the leading edge of migrating cells. We measured miR-9071 and SPAR1 in paired tumour and adjacent tissue, confirmed the interaction with luciferase reporters carrying the wild-type or a mutated SPAR1 3′ untranslated region, and tested the effect of miR-9071 mimics and inhibitors on SPAR1 protein, migration, invasion and proliferation in HepG2 and Huh7 cells. miR-9071 bound the SPAR1 3′ untranslated region and lowered SPAR1 protein, and its overexpression reduced migration and invasion. Restoring SPAR1 from a construct lacking the binding site reversed these effects. miR-9071 may therefore be a regulator of HCC cell motility worth further study.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary cancer of the liver and one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide. Most patients are diagnosed when the disease is already advanced, and even after resection or ablation a large share of patients develop intrahepatic recurrence within a few years. Recurrence and spread within the liver depend on the ability of tumour cells to detach, migrate through the surrounding matrix and enter the portal venous system, so the molecular machinery that drives HCC cell motility is a long-standing target of research.
Cell migration requires the coordinated reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton, the microtubule network and the adhesions that link the cell to its surroundings. Proteins first described in the mitotic spindle have repeatedly turned out to play a second role in interphase cells, where they organise microtubules at the cell cortex and help polarise the cell in the direction of movement. Several of these proteins are overexpressed in liver cancer, and high expression has been associated with poorer outcomes in retrospective cohorts.
SPAR1 (spindle-associated regulator 1) is one such protein. It binds microtubules during mitosis and localises to the spindle poles, but in non-dividing cells a fraction of SPAR1 is found at the leading edge, close to focal adhesions. Overexpression of SPAR1 has been reported in several solid tumours, and knock-down of SPAR1 reduces the motility of cultured cancer cells. How SPAR1 levels are controlled in HCC is not known.
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that repress gene expression after transcription, usually by binding to complementary sites in the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR) of their target messenger RNAs. A single microRNA can regulate dozens of targets, and the loss of tumour-suppressive microRNAs is a common feature of HCC. Many microRNAs reported in liver cancer act on regulators of the cytoskeleton and of epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
miR-9071 is a little-studied microRNA encoded in an intron of a gene expressed in hepatocytes. In a screen of public expression data we noticed that miR-9071 was among the microRNAs most reduced in HCC compared with non-tumour liver, and target prediction placed a conserved binding site for it in the 3′UTR of SPAR1. We therefore asked whether miR-9071 regulates SPAR1 in HCC cells, and whether this regulation affects their migration and invasion.

sections.heading: 2. Materials and methods
sections.text:
2.1 Tissue samples. Paired tumour and adjacent non-tumour liver tissue were obtained from patients undergoing hepatectomy for HCC at the institute's affiliated hospital. No patient had received chemotherapy or embolisation before surgery. Tissue was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen within 30 minutes of resection and stored at −80 °C. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee and every patient gave written informed consent. Clinical data were recorded from the hospital's records by a researcher who did not take part in the laboratory work.
2.2 Cell culture. The HCC cell lines HepG2 and Huh7 and the immortalised hepatocyte line used as a non-tumour control were obtained from a commercial cell bank and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium with 10% foetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in 5% CO₂, and were tested for mycoplasma every month. Experiments used cells within 15 passages of thawing.
2.3 Transfection. miR-9071 mimics, miR-9071 inhibitors and their matched negative controls were purchased from a commercial supplier and transfected at a final concentration of 50 nM using a lipid-based reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions. For rescue experiments, a SPAR1 coding sequence without its 3′UTR was cloned into an expression vector and co-transfected with the mimic; an empty vector served as control. Cells were harvested or assayed 48 hours after transfection unless stated otherwise.
2.4 RNA extraction and quantitative PCR. Total RNA, including small RNAs, was extracted with a column-based kit. miR-9071 was reverse transcribed with a stem-loop primer and quantified by TaqMan-style quantitative PCR, normalised to the small nuclear RNA U6. SPAR1 mRNA was quantified with SYBR Green chemistry and normalised to GAPDH. Relative expression was calculated with the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Each sample was run in triplicate.
2.5 Western blotting. Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes and probed with a rabbit anti-SPAR1 antibody and a mouse anti-β-actin antibody as loading control. Bands were detected by enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry. Uncropped blots are provided in the supplementary material.
2.6 Luciferase reporter assay. A fragment of the SPAR1 3′UTR containing the predicted miR-9071 site was cloned downstream of the firefly luciferase gene in a dual-luciferase reporter vector. A mutant reporter was made by changing four nucleotides of the seed-matching sequence. HEK293T cells were co-transfected with a reporter and either the miR-9071 mimic or the control mimic, and firefly activity was normalised to Renilla activity after 48 hours.
2.7 Migration and invasion assays. Migration was measured in Transwell chambers with 8 µm pores. Transfected cells were seeded in serum-free medium in the upper chamber, and medium with 10% serum was placed in the lower chamber. After 24 hours, cells on the lower surface were fixed, stained with crystal violet and counted in five random fields per membrane. Invasion was measured in the same way with chambers coated with basement membrane matrix, over 36 hours. Wound-healing assays were done on confluent monolayers scratched with a pipette tip and imaged at 0 and 24 hours.
2.8 Proliferation assay. Proliferation was measured with a colorimetric tetrazolium assay at 24, 48 and 72 hours after transfection, and by colony formation over 14 days.
2.9 Statistics. Each in vitro experiment was performed at least three times independently. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation. Two groups were compared with Student's t test (paired for tissue samples) and more than two with one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey's test. Correlation was assessed with Pearson's coefficient. P < 0.05 was considered significant. Counting of migrated cells was done by an observer blinded to the treatment group.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
3.1 miR-9071 is reduced and SPAR1 is increased in HCC tissue. We first measured miR-9071 in paired tumour and adjacent non-tumour tissue. miR-9071 was lower in most tumours than in the matching adjacent tissue, and SPAR1 mRNA showed the opposite pattern. Across the tumour samples, miR-9071 and SPAR1 mRNA levels were inversely correlated. Among the HCC cell lines, both HepG2 and Huh7 expressed less miR-9071 and more SPAR1 protein than the immortalised hepatocyte line, so both were used for the functional experiments.
3.2 miR-9071 binds the SPAR1 3′UTR. Target prediction identified one conserved site in the SPAR1 3′UTR that pairs with the seed region of miR-9071. In the reporter assay, the miR-9071 mimic reduced the luciferase activity of the wild-type reporter compared with the control mimic, while the activity of the mutant reporter, in which the seed-matching sequence had been changed, was not affected (Figure 1). This indicates that miR-9071 acts on SPAR1 through the predicted site.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Relative luciferase activity of the wild-type and mutant SPAR1 3′UTR reporters in HEK293T cells transfected with the miR-9071 mimic or the control mimic. Bars show mean ± SD of three independent experiments.

sections.text: 3.3 miR-9071 lowers SPAR1 protein in HCC cells. Transfection of the miR-9071 mimic raised miR-9071 levels in HepG2 and Huh7 cells, and the inhibitor lowered them, as confirmed by quantitative PCR. The mimic reduced SPAR1 protein in both cell lines, and the inhibitor increased it (Figure 2). SPAR1 mRNA changed in the same direction but to a smaller extent, consistent with a microRNA that acts partly by repressing translation.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Representative western blots of SPAR1 and β-actin in HepG2 and Huh7 cells transfected with the control mimic, the miR-9071 mimic, the control inhibitor or the miR-9071 inhibitor, with densitometry below.

sections.text: 3.4 miR-9071 reduces migration and invasion of HCC cells. We next tested whether miR-9071 affects the behaviour of HCC cells. In the Transwell assay, overexpression of miR-9071 reduced the migration of HepG2 cells by 48% compared with the control mimic (Table 2). Huh7 cells responded in the same direction. Matrix invasion was also reduced by the mimic in both cell lines, and wound closure at 24 hours was slower. Conversely, the miR-9071 inhibitor increased migration and invasion. Proliferation measured by the tetrazolium assay and colony formation did not differ between groups over the time course of the migration assays, so the reduction in migrated cells was not explained by fewer cells.

table.caption: Table 2. Transwell migration of HepG2 cells 48 h after transfection (cells per field, mean ± SD, three independent experiments).

sections.text: 3.5 Restoring SPAR1 reverses the effect of miR-9071. To test whether SPAR1 is the target through which miR-9071 acts on motility, we co-transfected the miR-9071 mimic with a SPAR1 construct lacking the 3′UTR, which cannot be bound by the microRNA. Re-expression of SPAR1 restored SPAR1 protein to the level of control cells and largely restored migration and invasion (Figure 3). The empty vector had no effect. These results suggest that the effect of miR-9071 on HCC cell motility is mediated, at least in large part, by SPAR1.

figure.caption: Figure 3. Transwell migration and invasion of HepG2 cells co-transfected with the miR-9071 mimic and either an empty vector or a SPAR1 construct lacking the 3′UTR. Representative fields above, counts below.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In this study we identify miR-9071 as a microRNA that is reduced in HCC tissue and that regulates SPAR1, a spindle-associated protein with a second role at the leading edge of migrating cells. miR-9071 bound a conserved site in the SPAR1 3′UTR, lowered SPAR1 protein, and reduced the migration and invasion of two HCC cell lines, and restoring SPAR1 from a construct the microRNA cannot bind reversed these effects.
These findings fit a wider picture in which mitotic proteins are reused by interphase cells to steer movement. Spindle-associated proteins that bind microtubule plus ends can capture microtubules at the cell cortex and stabilise them near focal adhesions, which helps a cell keep its direction of travel. If SPAR1 plays such a role in HCC cells, reducing its level would be expected to slow migration without necessarily affecting proliferation over a short period, which is what we observed.
The inverse relationship between miR-9071 and SPAR1 in tumour tissue supports the idea that the loss of miR-9071 contributes to high SPAR1 levels in HCC. However, a correlation in tissue cannot show causation, and other mechanisms, including gene amplification and transcriptional activation, may also raise SPAR1 in some tumours. Each microRNA also has many targets, and miR-9071 is likely to regulate other genes that affect motility.
Our study has limitations. All functional experiments were done in two cell lines in culture, and we did not test whether miR-9071 affects tumour spread in an animal model. The tissue cohort came from a single centre, and we did not relate miR-9071 levels to recurrence or survival. The mechanism by which SPAR1 promotes migration, and whether it depends on its microtubule-binding domain, remains to be worked out. Finally, the delivery of microRNA mimics to tumours remains a practical obstacle for any therapeutic use.
Despite these limitations, the results identify a microRNA–target pair that links a tumour-suppressive microRNA to a spindle protein involved in cell motility. Further work in animal models and larger patient cohorts will be needed to establish whether miR-9071 or SPAR1 could serve as markers of invasive disease or as targets for treatment.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: miR-9071 is reduced in HCC and directly targets SPAR1. By lowering SPAR1, miR-9071 restrains the migration and invasion of HCC cells in culture. The miR-9071–SPAR1 axis is a candidate for further study in models of HCC spread.

sections.heading: Data availability
sections.text: The data supporting the findings of this study, including uncropped blots and raw migration counts, are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Disclosure statement
sections.text: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors. This work was supported by a grant from the Fake Foundation for Liver Research.

documents.title: Retraction notice: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1
documents.text:
Retraction notice: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1

We, the Editor and Publisher of J. Fake Bioengineering, have retracted the above article. Following an investigation by the publisher into a group of articles, concerns were raised about the duplication of images. The article is therefore retracted. The retracted article will remain online to maintain the scholarly record, but it will be digitally watermarked on each page as RETRACTED.

documents.title: Statement of reinstatement: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1
documents.text:
Statement of reinstatement: MicroRNA-9071 suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma cell migration by targeting the spindle-associated regulator SPAR1

The retraction notice for the above article, published on 22 September 2026, was issued in error. The image concerns that led to the retraction relate to a different article in the same investigation, and this article was included by mistake. The publisher has checked the images and data of this article and found no problems with them. The retraction is withdrawn, the article is reinstated, and the RETRACTED watermark has been removed. We apologise to the authors and readers for this error.

draft_doc.running_head: Draft for supervisor review · not for circulation · November 2026
draft_doc.title: Spindle-associated proteins as drivers of hepatocellular carcinoma cell motility: a review and a proposed knock-down study
draft_doc.authors: Tan Jia Hui · Year 2 research project, Biomedical Engineering
draft_doc.abstract: Intrahepatic spread is the main reason that hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurs after treatment. This draft reviews the evidence that proteins first described in the mitotic spindle also drive the migration of cancer cells, and the evidence that microRNAs control their levels in liver cancer. It then proposes a small study in two HCC cell lines that tests whether lowering one such protein, SPAR1, slows migration, and whether a microRNA known to target it can do so as well. We set out the methods, the expected results and the limits of what the study can show.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer and remains one of the leading causes of cancer death [1]. Surgery and ablation can cure early disease, but recurrence within the liver is common, and much of it is thought to come from tumour cells that had already spread through the portal venous system before treatment [2, 3]. Slowing the movement of tumour cells is therefore an attractive complement to treatments that kill them.
Cell migration is a multi-step process. A moving cell must polarise, extend a protrusion at its front, form new adhesions, contract its body and release adhesions at its rear [4]. Each of these steps depends on the cytoskeleton. Actin filaments drive the protrusion itself, while microtubules provide direction: they deliver membrane, signalling proteins and adhesion regulators to the front of the cell and help to dismantle adhesions at the rear [5].
In epithelial cancers, the switch to a motile state often accompanies a partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition, in which cells lose tight junctions and gain mesenchymal markers [6]. In HCC this transition has been linked to vascular invasion and early recurrence [7]. Many of the proteins that change during this transition are themselves regulated by small non-coding RNAs, which makes the regulatory layer as interesting as the proteins [8].
This review focuses on one class of proteins that has received less attention in liver cancer than actin regulators: proteins first described as parts of the mitotic spindle that turn out to have a second job in interphase cells [9]. We first summarise what is known about their role in cell motility, then the evidence that microRNAs control them in HCC, and finally propose a short study that could be done with the equipment available in our laboratory.

sections.heading: 2. Spindle proteins outside mitosis
sections.text:
The mitotic spindle is built from microtubules and a large set of associated proteins that nucleate, stabilise, cross-link and move them [10]. For a long time these proteins were studied almost only in dividing cells. Over the last decade, however, a growing number of them have been found at the cortex of non-dividing cells, where they capture the plus ends of microtubules and anchor them near focal adhesions [11]. This capture is thought to help a migrating cell keep its direction of travel, because it biases the delivery of cargo to one side of the cell.
Several observations support a role for these proteins in cancer cell motility. First, many are overexpressed in solid tumours, often independently of the proliferation rate of the tumour [12]. Second, knock-down of individual proteins in cultured cancer cells slows migration in Transwell and wound-healing assays without immediately affecting proliferation [13]. Third, in some tumour types high expression is associated with vascular invasion in surgical specimens [15].
SPAR1 (spindle-associated regulator 1) is a good example. During mitosis it binds microtubules at the spindle poles, but in interphase cells a fraction of it is found at the leading edge, close to focal adhesions [16]. SPAR1 is overexpressed in several solid tumours, and knock-down of SPAR1 slows the motility of cultured cancer cells [17]. Its role in liver cancer has received less attention, and how its level is controlled in HCC cells is only beginning to be studied.
It is important to separate effects on motility from effects on cell number. Because spindle proteins are needed for division, reducing them could in principle lower the number of cells that reach the lower side of a Transwell membrane simply because fewer cells are present. Studies that measure proliferation over the same period as the migration assay, and that use short assays, can rule this out [18]. We return to this point in the proposed methods.

sections.heading: 3. MicroRNA control of spindle proteins in HCC
sections.text:
MicroRNAs are short RNAs that repress their target genes, usually by pairing with sites in the 3′ untranslated region of the target messenger RNA [19]. The loss of tumour-suppressive microRNAs is a common event in HCC, and several of the microRNAs lost in liver tumours act on regulators of the cytoskeleton [20]. Because one microRNA can act on many targets, restoring a single lost microRNA can change several pathways at once, which is both an opportunity and a complication for interpreting experiments [21].
The clearest evidence that a microRNA controls SPAR1 in liver cancer comes from Liang et al. [14]. They found that miR-9071 is reduced in HCC tissue compared with adjacent liver, showed with luciferase reporters that it binds a conserved site in the SPAR1 3′ untranslated region, and found that a miR-9071 mimic lowered SPAR1 protein in HepG2 and Huh7 cells. In their Transwell assay, overexpression of miR-9071 reduced the migration of HepG2 cells by 48%, and re-expressing SPAR1 from a construct the microRNA cannot bind largely restored migration [14]. This is the main finding our proposed study builds on: it gives both a target worth knocking down and a positive control for the effect of lowering it.
Two features of that work make it a useful starting point. First, the rescue experiment links the effect of the microRNA to SPAR1 itself rather than to its other targets. Second, proliferation was measured over the same period as the migration assay and did not differ between groups, which addresses the concern raised in Section 2 [14]. What the study did not do was test the effect of lowering SPAR1 directly, without the microRNA, or test whether the effect holds in a three-dimensional matrix closer to liver tissue [22].

sections.heading: 4. Proposed study
sections.text:
Aim. To test whether direct knock-down of SPAR1 slows the migration and invasion of HCC cells as much as the miR-9071 mimic does, and whether the effect holds in a three-dimensional spheroid invasion assay.
Cells and treatments. HepG2 and Huh7 cells will be cultured under standard conditions [23]. Four groups will be compared in each cell line: a control small interfering RNA, a SPAR1 small interfering RNA, a control mimic and a miR-9071 mimic, with the mimic conditions following Liang et al. [14] so that their result serves as our positive control. Knock-down will be confirmed by quantitative PCR and western blotting 48 hours after transfection.
Assays. Migration will be measured in Transwell chambers over 24 hours and invasion in matrix-coated chambers over 36 hours, as in the published protocol [14, 24]. In addition, spheroids will be embedded in a collagen matrix and the area invaded at 48 hours measured from images. Proliferation will be measured over the same periods so that effects on migration can be separated from effects on cell number [18]. Counting will be done blind to group.
Analysis. Each experiment will be repeated three times. Groups will be compared by one-way analysis of variance with Tukey's test. Our primary comparison is SPAR1 knock-down against control small interfering RNA; the secondary comparison is SPAR1 knock-down against the miR-9071 mimic.

sections.heading: 5. Expected results and limitations
sections.text:
If SPAR1 is the main route by which miR-9071 slows HCC cells, direct knock-down should reduce migration and invasion by a similar amount to the mimic, and the spheroid assay should show less invasion into the matrix. If knock-down has a smaller effect than the mimic, other targets of the microRNA probably contribute, which would fit the general picture of microRNAs acting on networks rather than single genes [21].
The study has clear limits. Two cell lines grown on plastic are a long way from a tumour in a liver, and neither the Transwell nor the spheroid assay reproduces the portal venous system through which HCC spreads [25]. Small interfering RNAs have off-target effects, so a second independent sequence will be used if time allows [26]. The study cannot say anything about whether SPAR1 levels predict recurrence in patients, which would require a clinical cohort [27]. Finally, any therapeutic use would face the well-known problem of delivering RNA to tumours [28].

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: Spindle-associated proteins are emerging as regulators of cancer cell motility, and the microRNA miR-9071 has been shown to control one of them, SPAR1, in HCC cells. The proposed study would test SPAR1 directly and in a more tissue-like assay, using the published miR-9071 result as its positive control. If it confirms the effect, the next step would be an animal model of intrahepatic spread [29].

must_include: says the retraction was issued in error and has been withdrawn, with the paper reinstated
says the paper's findings or data can still be relied on
must_not_include: treats the paper as still retracted or tells the researcher to stop citing it
says the paper's images or data were found to be duplicated or unreliable

expected.why: Rubric: the report's severity is lower than its highest alert when a later notice resolves an earlier one. The later notice says the retraction "was issued in error", that "the article is reinstated" and that the publisher "found no problems" with its images and data, so the retraction is resolved like a lifted concern (case 17) and the report is none. Crossref has no reinstatement type, so the pipeline keeps the high retraction alert (key retraction) and raises the reinstatement only as a medium other:addendum alert; a model that just takes the highest alert says high (RE-changes-explained.md §1, R8; §7 item 13). Severity none stops the pipeline before the draft is read.
